title: Connected scatterplots: preserve time order, gaps and trajectory direction
summary: Trace paired measurements through the X–Y plane without inventing observations across missing periods or interpreting loops as proof of causation.
body:
Trace paired measurements through the X–Y plane without inventing observations across missing periods or interpreting loops as proof of causation.

Make two measures and one clock explicit

A connected scatterplot places one quantitative measure on the horizontal axis and another on the vertical axis, then joins observations in chronological order. Time is encoded by the path rather than either axis. That separates it from an ordinary time-series line chart, whose horizontal axis is time, and from an unconnected scatterplot, which contains no ordered journey. Use it when the question concerns how two measures move together across successive periods: did both rise, did one lead the other, and did the system return to a former combination? Put the units, measurement grain and time-step rule next to the chart. Two plotted values must refer to the same entity and period; pairing this week's costs with last week's outcomes by accident can create a false loop. Chart encoding, grain rules and period alignment should be fixed first.

Order the path by time, never by X value

Many plotting libraries connect points in input order. A database result without an explicit time sort can therefore produce a different path on a second run. Sort by a unique, declared period key and reject duplicate observations unless the aggregation policy specifies how to combine them. Mark the start and end, add sparse period labels and draw direction arrows where a reversal would otherwise be ambiguous. An arrow points forward through time, not necessarily toward increasing X or Y. Keep both numeric axes stable across compared groups. If a measure can be negative, retain a meaningful zero line when that helps interpretation; do not force both axes to zero merely to fill a square frame. The worked contract returns ordered points and allowable segments so a renderer cannot accidentally reorder them. Axis integrity and shared-scale panels protect comparisons.

Break at unobserved periods

A straight segment from period 48 to period 50 suggests a continuous movement through the middle even when period 49 was never measured. Break the line at that gap or draw a distinctly styled connection with a documented interpolation rule. The simple contract below only connects consecutive integer periods. It leaves points after a gap visible but starts a new path. For irregular calendars, a consecutive integer is not enough: use an explicit sequence of expected periods that incorporates holidays, fiscal weeks or excluded maintenance windows. A blank period is not a zero measurement. Nor should the line skip a failed sensor silently. Show completeness counts and use a companion pair of ordinary time-series charts when it matters which variable changed during a gap. Calendar and provisional-period rules describe that boundary.

Read shape without claiming a mechanism

A path heading northeast means both measures increased between adjacent observations. A loop means the pair revisited a part of the X–Y plane after taking a different route. It may be consistent with lag, seasonality, changed population mix or measurement timing; the shape alone cannot choose among them. Large jumps can dominate the path and hide small movements, while overlapping segments can make direction hard to follow. Annotate major period boundaries, then test the story against the original separate time series. If many entities are present, one dense web is rarely legible; use a few labeled trajectories or small multiples. Avoid animation as the only route to chronology, and provide an ordered table of period, X and Y. Animation controls, accessible text and causal-claim limits remain relevant.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def paired_trajectory(readings: list[tuple[int, float, float]]):
    if not readings:
        raise ValueError("at least one paired period is required")
    seen = set()
    for period, acquisition_cost, activation_rate in readings:
        if (not isinstance(period, int) or period in seen or
                not isfinite(acquisition_cost) or acquisition_cost < 0 or
                not isfinite(activation_rate) or not 0 <= activation_rate <= 1):
            raise ValueError("periods must be unique; paired measures must be valid")
        seen.add(period)
    points = sorted(readings)
    segments = [(earlier, later)
                for earlier, later in zip(points, points[1:])
                if later[0] == earlier[0] + 1]
    gaps = [(earlier[0], later[0])
            for earlier, later in zip(points, points[1:])
            if later[0] != earlier[0] + 1]
    return points, segments, gaps

weekly_acquisition = [(50, 83.0, 0.59), (47, 71.0, 0.47),
                      (48, 79.0, 0.53), (51, 77.0, 0.64)]
points, segments, gaps = paired_trajectory(weekly_acquisition)
assert [period for period, _, _ in points] == [47, 48, 50, 51]
assert [(start[0], end[0]) for start, end in segments] == [(47, 48), (50, 51)]
assert gaps == [(48, 50)]
assert points[-1][2] == 0.64

Performance and operating cost

For N paired periods, validation takes O(N) expected time, sorting takes O(N log N), and segment construction takes O(N). The duplicate-key set, sorted points and segment ledger use O(N) space. In the worked data, the input arrives out of order, but the output orders periods 47, 48, 50 and 51. The chart draws segments from 47 to 48 and from 50 to 51; it refuses to suggest an observed route through missing period 49. The activation rate rises to 0.64 by the final period even though acquisition cost falls from 83 to 77 between 50 and 51. Those are adjacent descriptive changes, not an estimated causal effect.

Common Mistakes

  • Connecting points in database-return order or sorting by the horizontal measure.
  • Pairing measures from different cohorts or period definitions.
  • Drawing a solid segment through an unobserved period without an interpolation rule.
  • Calling a loop evidence that one measure caused a delayed change in the other.

Validation drill

Track 83 weekly cost and activation pairs for one stable cohort. Audit duplicate weeks, mark every break in the expected calendar, label start and end, then compare the trajectory with two ordinary time-series charts before interpreting a loop.

title: Missingness matrices: reveal record-order patterns and co-missing fields
summary: Build a binary presence matrix with explicit null rules, row order, pattern counts and field-pair support before imputing or dropping records.
body:
Build a binary presence matrix with explicit null rules, row order, pattern counts and field-pair support before imputing or dropping records.

Treat presence as a separate variable

A missingness matrix displays records on one axis and fields on the other, coloring each cell according to whether the field was observed. Its first job is to show structure hidden by overall missing percentages: a whole block lost during one import, one field absent only for a particular cohort, or two fields disappearing together. Define missing before plotting. In this lesson, None and floating-point NaN are missing; zero and an empty string count as observed values unless a separate domain rule says otherwise. That rule must be applied before rendering and recorded with the chart, because changing it can redraw the pattern without changing any source records. An imputed value is not originally observed and should retain a separate provenance flag. Heatmap missing-cell encoding and dashboard provenance support that distinction.

Keep the row order meaningful

A random row order can turn a sustained outage into a scattered texture. Sort records by acquisition time, batch ID or another declared operational sequence, and retain stable unique row identifiers. A secondary sort by missingness pattern can reveal common combinations but destroys chronology; if you use it, label the new order and keep a time-ordered companion view. At large N, drawing every row may produce thousands of subpixel cells. Aggregate into windows, sample with a fixed documented rule, or summarize repeated patterns; never hide rare but consequential failures in an average. Show row count and per-field observed counts beside the matrix. If batches have different schemas, use an explicit not-applicable state rather than treating structurally absent fields as ordinary missing data. Level of detail and time gaps determine how much the reader can see.

Count patterns and pair overlap, not just column rates

Two fields may each be missing in a quarter of records yet fail in completely different rows. A matrix shows the difference; pattern frequencies and pairwise co-missing counts quantify it. The code creates a boolean mask per row, counts each exact pattern, and counts records in which every selected pair is missing. These pair counts are not a correlation coefficient and cannot by themselves explain why values are absent. Show the denominator for every pair: records eligible for both fields. If eligibility changes across rows, restrict the calculation to comparable records or add explicit applicability flags. A pair with no missing records has zero co-missing count, but a field that is always missing cannot be assessed for variation. Pairwise coverage and denominator policy prevent false comparisons.

Do not infer a missing-data mechanism from color blocks

A matrix can expose dependence on observed batches or fields, but it cannot prove that values are missing completely at random, missing at random conditional on observed variables, or missing not at random. The last case depends on unseen values, which the chart cannot display. Avoid turning a visually coherent pattern into an imputation rule without investigating the collection process and validating the downstream model. A form redesign, sensor outage, consent rule or ETL change can all create similar bands. Keep collection timestamps and data-quality events available for annotation; compare raw and post-cleaning views so deletion does not make failure disappear. Use a text table of missing rates, frequent patterns and affected periods for readers who cannot parse a dense matrix. Event annotations and text alternatives keep interpretation bounded.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from itertools import combinations
from math import isnan

FIELDS = ("order_total", "delivery_zone", "carrier_id")

def absent(value):
    return value is None or (isinstance(value, float) and isnan(value))

def missingness_ledger(records: list[tuple[int, str, dict]]):
    seen = set()
    matrix = []
    pattern_counts = Counter()
    pair_counts = Counter()
    missing_by_field = Counter()
    for period, order_id, values in records:
        if (not isinstance(period, int) or not order_id or order_id in seen or
                set(values) != set(FIELDS)):
            raise ValueError("rows need unique IDs and the declared schema")
        seen.add(order_id)
        missing = tuple(field for field in FIELDS if absent(values[field]))
        pattern_counts[missing] += 1
        missing_by_field.update(missing)
        pair_counts.update(combinations(missing, 2))
        matrix.append((period, order_id, tuple(field in missing for field in FIELDS)))
    matrix.sort(key=lambda row: (row[0], row[1]))
    return matrix, missing_by_field, pattern_counts, pair_counts

orders = [(50, "order-83", {"order_total": 83.0, "delivery_zone": None,
                             "carrier_id": None}),
          (47, "order-47", {"order_total": 47.0, "delivery_zone": "W",
                             "carrier_id": "carrier-7"}),
          (48, "order-59", {"order_total": float("nan"),
                             "delivery_zone": "E", "carrier_id": None}),
          (51, "order-97", {"order_total": 0.0, "delivery_zone": "",
                             "carrier_id": "carrier-9"})]
matrix, field_counts, patterns, pairs = missingness_ledger(orders)
assert [row[0] for row in matrix] == [47, 48, 50, 51]
assert field_counts == {"order_total": 1, "delivery_zone": 1, "carrier_id": 2}
assert pairs[("delivery_zone", "carrier_id")] == 1
assert patterns[()] == 2
assert matrix[-1][2] == (False, False, False)

Performance and operating cost

For N records and K declared fields, building masks and field counts takes O(NK) time. Counting every missing pair takes O(sum mᵢ²), at most O(NK²), where mᵢ is the number of missing fields in row i; sorting the row ledger adds O(N log N). Matrix storage is O(NK), while pattern and pair counters can reach O(min(N, 2ᴷ) plus K²) entries. The sample has four orders, two fully observed patterns, one missing total, one missing zone and two missing carrier IDs. Only one record loses both zone and carrier. Its final record's zero total and empty zone remain observed under the declared rule; another business rule could mark the empty zone missing, but must be versioned and disclosed.

Common Mistakes

  • Conflating zero, empty string, NaN, None and not-applicable without a field contract.
  • Sorting rows by missingness and then describing a resulting band as chronological.
  • Interpreting co-missing counts as a causal mechanism or a formal correlation measure.
  • Removing bad records before charting and presenting the cleaned matrix as raw quality evidence.

Validation drill

Audit 83 ordered import batches with three required fields and one optional field. Publish raw missingness patterns, per-field support and the most common co-missing pair; keep not-applicable separate and annotate any schema or collection change.

  • Correlation heatmaps: show pairwise coverage before interpreting color
  • Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
  • Dashboard filters and provenance: make every view reproducible

title: Data Visualization Tutorial
summary: Design auditable charts from explicit populations, stable scales, visible uncertainty and accessible representations.
body:

body:
Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.

Where to begin

Start with the decision a reader must make. Then choose an encoding that preserves the relevant comparison, define the aggregation grain, and check scale, distribution, small samples, accessibility, and dashboard provenance. The linked project turns those choices into a reviewable operations display.

A chart with many filters can become expensive to compute and hard to interpret. Pre-aggregate only at a grain that preserves the intended question, and state when a denominator or sample size changes under a filter.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Event-aligned charts: choose a baseline before comparing trajectories
summary: Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.
body:
Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.

Event time is not calendar time

An event-aligned chart puts each subject's event at relative time zero. This lets a reader compare trajectories before and after events that occurred on different calendar dates. Store the actual event timestamp as well as the relative offset; otherwise seasonality, outages and policy changes disappear. Specify whether an offset means elapsed hours, calendar days or complete reporting periods. Time-series period rules are essential when the event occurs late in a day or across a daylight-saving change.

Fix the baseline rule

A common display subtracts each subject's pre-event value or divides by it. These produce different shapes and units. Select the baseline window before inspecting outcomes, report how many valid observations contributed to it, and reject a percentage change when the baseline is zero. If one subject has only one pre-event measurement and another has 47, their aligned curves carry different reliability. Denominator and grain rules should stay visible with the chart. Plot absolute values alongside normalized values when the magnitude of the original series matters.

Missing is not flat

Do not fill missing pre-event days with the baseline or connect a line across an unobserved outage without a marker. A cohort average at relative day five may use fewer subjects than at day one because follow-up ends; show the contributing count by offset. Attrition can make a trend look like improvement. Small-sample uncertainty belongs near sparse tails, and forecast intervals must not be substituted for missing actual observations.

The line does not prove an effect

A change at time zero can reflect selection into the event, a concurrent intervention, regression to the mean or ordinary seasonality. An annotation identifies timing, not causality. Compare a relevant untreated group or a pre-specified benchmark if the decision requires an effect estimate, and state the assumptions of that comparison. Annotation and causal-claim boundaries apply here. Export subject ID, event date, relative offset, original value, baseline window, normalized value and eligibility state so every plotted line can be reconstructed.

Worked contract

from datetime import date
from math import isfinite

def event_aligned_change(event_day: date, observations: dict[date, float],
                         baseline_days: tuple[date, ...]
                        ) -> list[tuple[int, float, float]]:
    if not baseline_days or len(set(baseline_days)) != len(baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline days must be distinct")
    if any(day >= event_day or day not in observations for day in baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline must be observed before the event")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in observations.values()):
        raise ValueError("observations must be finite")
    baseline = sum(observations[day] for day in baseline_days) / len(baseline_days)
    return sorted(((day - event_day).days, value, value - baseline)
                  for day, value in observations.items())

incident_counts = {
    date(2026, 10, 5): 47, date(2026, 10, 6): 59,
    date(2026, 10, 8): 38, date(2026, 10, 9): 35,
}
aligned = event_aligned_change(
    date(2026, 10, 7), incident_counts,
    (date(2026, 10, 5), date(2026, 10, 6)),
)
assert aligned == [(-2, 47, -6), (-1, 59, 6), (1, 38, -15), (2, 35, -18)]
assert all(offset != 0 for offset, _, _ in aligned)

Performance and operating cost

For N observations and B baseline days, validation and averaging take O(N+B) time; sorting relative periods takes O(N log N) time and O(N) output space. The function leaves missing event day zero absent instead of inventing a value. Calendar dates are appropriate only when day-level reporting is the contract; intraday events need zoned timestamps and a declared binning method. Subtracting a baseline describes change, not a causal estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Discarding calendar dates after alignment and losing concurrent-event context.
  • Choosing a favorable baseline window after seeing the result.
  • Drawing a continuous line over days with no observations.
  • Calling a post-event change proof that the event caused it.

Validation drill

Align 81 facilities around a maintenance intervention. Show each facility's baseline window and post-event coverage, then recompute the cohort curve using only facilities observed through day 14.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

Validation drill

Facet five depot delay series on one weekly calendar. Produce a shared-scale view for absolute comparison and a labeled independent-scale view for within-depot variation; write down which conclusions differ.

title: Chart annotations: align events to the right clock without claiming causality
summary: Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.
body:
Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.

An annotation is another dataset

A vertical line on a chart often marks a deployment, policy change or outage. That event has its own timestamp, time zone, scope, source and uncertainty. A release may roll through regions over several hours; drawing one instant across all regions invents precision. Model it as a window or per-region events, then map it to the same clock as the measured series. The time-series clock must be settled before annotations are placed.

Scope must match the measured population

If only one depot received a new workflow, an all-depot annotation can imply that every plotted change followed the intervention. Filter event records by affected site, product and population, and expose the scope in the label. Preserve events outside the visible interval in the export but do not draw them in the viewport. Distinguish a data outage from a true operational incident: both can create a cliff, but only one is a measured outcome. Population contracts determine whether a note belongs on a chart.

Timing does not prove effect

A change in the curve after a marked event may be coincidence, seasonality, a denominator shift or a delayed measurement. Write labels such as 'workflow enabled' rather than 'workflow improved response time' unless a separate analysis supports the latter. If an effect is being estimated, show the design, comparison group and uncertainty elsewhere. Effect-size analysis is distinct from descriptive annotation. Keep the event visible even when the post-event result disappoints expectations.

Avoid collision and preserve provenance

Several events on one day can produce overlapping labels. Group them in a visible list keyed to markers, prioritizing material scope and preserving access to every event. The annotation export should include event ID, earliest and latest time, scope, label and source version. A revised event time should update the chart and its manifest together. Reproducible exports need both series and annotation versions. Test daylight-saving boundaries and a deployment window that straddles the chart's range.

Worked contract

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def visible_events(
    events: list[tuple[str, datetime, datetime, set[str]]],
    view_start: datetime, view_end: datetime, depot_id: str
) -> list[str]:
    if view_start.tzinfo is None or view_end.tzinfo is None or view_start >= view_end:
        raise ValueError("invalid aware view interval")
    selected = []
    for event_id, began, ended, depots in events:
        if not event_id or began.tzinfo is None or ended.tzinfo is None or began >= ended:
            raise ValueError("invalid event interval")
        if depot_id in depots and began < view_end and ended > view_start:
            selected.append(event_id)
    return selected

utc = timezone.utc
window = [("release-47", datetime(2026, 8, 11, 9, tzinfo=utc),
           datetime(2026, 8, 11, 11, tzinfo=utc), {"north"})]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "north") == ["release-47"]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "south") == []

Performance and operating cost

Scanning E events is O(E) time and O(M) output space for M matching IDs. An indexed event store can narrow by time and scope for many dashboards. The example uses half-open display intervals and event windows, so a window ending exactly at the view start is excluded. It does not infer causality or validate whether a deployment reached every unit in its declared scope; those are separate evidence checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a gradual rollout as one global instant.
  • Annotating all depots with an event that affected only one.
  • Writing a causal outcome claim in an event label without a study.
  • Failing to version corrected event times alongside the plotted series.

Validation drill

Annotate a 29-day response-time chart with three region-specific rollouts, one data outage and one event that crosses the visible interval boundary. Verify the right events appear for each region and export their time windows.

title: Heatmaps: make missing cells, rates and color domains explicit
summary: Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.
body:
Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.

A cell needs two keys and one measure

A heatmap is a matrix of marks whose position comes from two discrete dimensions and whose fill encodes a value. The first decision is the unit of a cell: one depot-day, one product-hour, or one model-class pair. Build the complete expected key grid before coloring it. Otherwise an absent record disappears, compresses the layout, or is mistaken for a low value. A white cell may mean zero, unobserved, unavailable or suppressed; these states require separate labels or patterns. Calendar completeness matters when columns are days.

Rates need their denominators

A defect-rate cell with 4 defects in 8 inspections and another with 40 in 800 inspections should not be interpreted as equally reliable even if their colors reflect 50% and 5%. Carry inspected count into a tooltip, visible annotation, or companion display. If no inspections occurred, the rate is undefined rather than zero. Measure grain determines whether the numerator and denominator belong to the same cell. If filters remove rows, recompute both counts instead of averaging precomputed cell percentages.

Fix the color domain for comparison

An automatically rescaled palette can make the same value change color when the viewer filters a subset. For cross-filter or before-after comparisons, set a stable domain and show its endpoints. A sequential palette fits a nonnegative rate; a diverging palette needs a meaningful center such as zero difference or target variance. Quantile coloring gives bins with similar record counts, not equal numeric widths. Label the bin rule. Accessible encodings add text or pattern cues so the chart still works without color.

Choose ordering deliberately

Alphabetical row order is reproducible, but ordering by a stable baseline can expose patterns. Clustering rows by similarity can reveal structure yet change the question: adjacent rows no longer imply geographic or operational proximity. If an algorithm orders rows, record its input period and freeze the order for comparisons. Keep hidden categories and totals visible. A truncated matrix that shows only the busiest depots is a selected population, not the entire network. Facet-order discipline applies here too.

Test the matrix contract

Include an observed zero, a missing key, a present key with zero exposure, an invalid negative count and a high-rate low-volume cell. Confirm each has a distinct state. Check the matrix against a long-form data table with the same row and column order. On mobile, provide axis labels that remain visible while scrolling; a distant legend is not enough. Exported CSV should retain status, numerator and denominator rather than only a color code.

Worked contract

def inspection_matrix(
    observations: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[int, int]],
    depots: list[str], days: list[str]
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[str, float | None, int | None]]:
    expected = {(depot, day) for depot in depots for day in days}
    if len(expected) != len(depots) * len(days) or set(observations) - expected:
        raise ValueError("duplicate labels or unexpected cell")
    grid = {}
    for key in expected:
        if key not in observations:
            grid[key] = ("missing", None, None)
            continue
        defects, inspected = observations[key]
        if not 0 <= defects <= inspected:
            raise ValueError("invalid cell counts")
        grid[key] = ("no-exposure", None, 0) if inspected == 0 else (
            "observed", defects / inspected, inspected)
    return grid

matrix = inspection_matrix(
    {("north", "Mon"): (0, 47), ("north", "Tue"): (0, 0)},
    ["north"], ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"])
assert matrix[("north", "Mon")] == ("observed", 0.0, 47)
assert matrix[("north", "Tue")][0] == "no-exposure"
assert matrix[("north", "Wed")][0] == "missing"

Performance and operating cost

For R row labels, C column labels and M supplied observations, building the expected grid takes O(RC + M) time and O(RC) space. Large sparse matrices should keep sparse storage and generate only visible tiles, but must still represent missing cells and axis positions correctly. The demonstration returns status, rate and denominator; a production export should also retain the numerator and source snapshot. Color scaling and rendering add work proportional to visible cells, not merely to supplied observations.

Common Mistakes

  • Assigning the same white fill to an observed zero and an absent cell.
  • Changing the color domain after filtering without warning the reader.
  • Averaging cell percentages instead of recomputing counts for a new group.
  • Sorting rows by one selected day, then describing the layout as a stable geographic order.

Validation drill

Build a depot-by-day inspection matrix with 6 depots and 17 days. Insert one missing cell, one zero-exposure cell and one observed zero. Verify their states in both chart legend and exported data.

title: Correlation heatmaps: show pairwise coverage before interpreting color
summary: Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.
body:
Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.

The matrix has more than coefficients

A correlation cell describes observations shared by two variables. With missing fields, one cell may use 810 records and another 47; identical color saturation hides that difference. Carry a second matrix of pairwise counts and expose it in labels, tooltips or a companion table. A blank pair means insufficient shared records or an undefined statistic, not zero association. Missing-cell rules distinguish these states. Record which rows passed eligibility filters before calculating either matrix.

Choose a missing-data contract

Pairwise deletion uses every available pair but can give each cell a different population. Complete-case deletion holds one population constant but may discard most records and change who remains. State the choice and counts. A constant column has zero variance and no Pearson correlation; mark it undefined. Do not fill its cell with zero merely to complete a square. Dataset grain and join checks should precede calculation so duplicated rows do not inflate confidence.

Order features for the reading task

Alphabetical order is stable and auditable. A domain order groups related measures. Data-driven clustering can reveal blocks, but the clustering method and input matrix become part of the result; changing order between periods makes comparison harder. Fix order for side-by-side charts, or record the exact order for each export. Show a legend centered on zero with identical limits in every panel. Scale integrity prevents a weak coefficient from receiving the same shade as a strong one elsewhere.

Do not infer a mechanism

A large coefficient can arise from shared time trends, repeated entities, selection or a third variable. The matrix is a screen for questions, not proof that changing one field changes another. Confirm striking cells with paired scatter plots, units and source counts; outliers can dominate a linear coefficient. Avoid painting both triangles when space is tight, since the duplicate area adds no information. Dense scatter views help inspect what the matrix compressed. Describe the population and time range beside every matrix.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def pearson_pair(records: list[dict[str, float | None]],
                 left: str, right: str) -> tuple[float | None, int]:
    pairs = [(record[left], record[right]) for record in records
             if record.get(left) is not None and record.get(right) is not None]
    count = len(pairs)
    if count < 2:
        return None, count
    left_mean = sum(value[0] for value in pairs) / count
    right_mean = sum(value[1] for value in pairs) / count
    cross = sum((x - left_mean) * (y - right_mean) for x, y in pairs)
    left_square = sum((x - left_mean) ** 2 for x, _ in pairs)
    right_square = sum((y - right_mean) ** 2 for _, y in pairs)
    if not left_square or not right_square:
        return None, count
    return cross / sqrt(left_square * right_square), count

shipments = [{"distance": 47, "cost": 81},
             {"distance": 59, "cost": 97},
             {"distance": 71, "cost": 113},
             {"distance": 83, "cost": None}]
coefficient, paired_count = pearson_pair(shipments, "distance", "cost")
assert round(coefficient, 12) == 1 and paired_count == 3

Performance and operating cost

For P fields and N rows, a direct full matrix performs O(P²N) pair work and stores O(P²) coefficients and counts. Columnar execution can lower constant costs, but pairwise coverage still needs explicit accounting. The example returns undefined for insufficient pairs or constant values and does not provide a significance test. A precise coefficient on three shared rows is weak evidence for a broad population claim.

Common Mistakes

  • Showing a coefficient without its pairwise record count.
  • Coloring undefined correlations as zero.
  • Changing row order across comparison periods without notice.
  • Treating a strong correlation as a causal intervention result.

Validation drill

Build a five-field matrix where one field appears in only 47 of 810 records. Show the count matrix beside the coefficient matrix, then compare pairwise and complete-case populations.

title: Dashboard filters and provenance: make every view reproducible
summary: A dashboard is a family of data queries; each control changes the population and needs an explicit, inspectable state.
body:
A dashboard is a family of data queries; each control changes the population and needs an explicit, inspectable state.

Version the query state

A screenshot of a 74 percent review rate means little without period, channel, eligibility version and data-refresh time. Encode those fields in a shareable state record. If a filter changes the cohort, recompute counts and intervals rather than carrying cached percentages across populations. The denominator must travel with every filtered value.

Manage defaults

A default “last 30 days” view moves each day. Use a fixed reporting cutoff for reproducible review packets and mark live periods provisional. If the dashboard initially excludes low-volume channels, disclose that exclusion rather than implying the total includes all channels. Make “all eligible channels” a testable state.

Prevent stale joins

A filter change may return fast chart data while the companion table or alternative text still shows the previous request. Apply response IDs or cancellation to keep all representations synchronized. The data pipeline should expose snapshot ID and query version. Publication boundaries offer a model for replacing a complete snapshot atomically.

Reproduce a decision

Save a review packet with filter state, metric definition, source snapshot, numerator, denominator and chart version. Re-run it after a late receipt arrives; the old packet must remain explainable even if the live dashboard changes. Test an invalid channel and a period with no eligible receipts rather than silently falling back to another state.

Implementation

def dashboard_state(snapshot_id, start_day, end_day, channels):
    if not snapshot_id or start_day >= end_day:
        raise ValueError("invalid snapshot or period")
    selected = tuple(sorted(set(channels)))
    if not selected:
        raise ValueError("select at least one channel")
    return {"snapshot_id": snapshot_id, "start_day": start_day,
            "end_day": end_day, "channels": selected}

Performance and operating cost

Canonicalizing C selected channels costs O(C log C) time and O(C) space. Query and render costs depend on the backend and mark count; a versioned aggregate cache can help, but its key must include every population-changing filter.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not publish a decision screenshot without snapshot and filter state.
  • Do not reuse an overall interval after changing the cohort.
  • Do not let chart, table and alternative text resolve different query responses.

title: Large chart series: reduce marks without erasing spikes
summary: Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.
body:
Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.

More samples than pixels need a display rule

A line chart with hundreds of thousands of readings across a 900-pixel plot cannot show each reading distinctly. Sending every point still costs transfer, parsing, memory, layout and interaction time. A random sample or every-50th-point stride can erase a brief but operationally important spike. Decide whether the reader is inspecting shape, extrema, exact intervals or anomalies. The chart task determines the reduction method. The full-resolution data remains the source; the plotted series is a deliberately derived view.

Preserve a bounded envelope

For each time bucket, retain its first, last, minimum and maximum observations, ordered by timestamp and deduplicated by identity. This keeps endpoints connected and exposes local peaks and troughs that a mean would smooth away. It is not lossless: the order of several internal turns and narrow oscillations may still be compressed. Show the bucket width or resolution when it affects interpretation, and fetch raw samples on zoom or request. If missing intervals exist, split segments before reducing; joining across a gap creates a fictional line. Gap policy applies before level of detail.

Build levels against stable data versions

Precomputed hourly, daily or pixel-width buckets must use a fixed time origin and a named aggregation function. If a late event revises an old bucket, invalidate that level together with raw data. Cache keys need range, resolution, filters, unit and source generation. A multi-resolution chart can request a coarser level during pan, then replace it with fine points after the interaction settles; label provisional rendering when it might change a decision. Serving freshness constrains what a pre-aggregated chart can claim.

Keep exactness available

Tooltips on reduced marks should describe the bucket, extrema and sample count. Calling a retained minimum a point-in-time average is wrong. A downloadable CSV should offer the filtered raw interval or clearly name the reduced level. If a user clicks a peak to investigate a machine stoppage, resolve it to source IDs rather than an arbitrary nearby display point. The export manifest should state whether the series is raw or reduced.

Measure end-to-end cost

Track transfer bytes, parse time, memory, first paint, pan latency and number of marks actually drawn. A server-side envelope can reduce browser work but adds query and cache-maintenance cost. A canvas renderer can draw many marks faster than DOM-based SVG, yet it needs deliberate keyboard and text alternatives. Test a single-sample range, identical timestamps, gaps and a narrow spike at each bucket boundary. The acceptance check is not only a speedup: the operational alert must remain visible at the default zoom.

Worked contract

def extrema_envelope(samples: list[tuple[int, float]],
                     bucket_size: int) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    if bucket_size < 1 or any(samples[index][0] >= samples[index + 1][0]
                               for index in range(len(samples) - 1)):
        raise ValueError("bucket size or time order is invalid")
    reduced = []
    for start in range(0, len(samples), bucket_size):
        bucket = samples[start:start + bucket_size]
        selected = {bucket[0], bucket[-1],
                    min(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1]),
                    max(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1])}
        reduced.extend(sorted(selected, key=lambda point: point[0]))
    return reduced

readings = [(47, 4.0), (48, 4.1), (49, 81.0), (50, 4.2),
            (51, 4.0), (52, 3.9)]
visible = extrema_envelope(readings, 4)
assert (49, 81.0) in visible and visible[0] == readings[0]
assert len(visible) <= 4 * ((len(readings) + 3) // 4)

Performance and operating cost

For N sorted samples and bucket size B, the demonstration runs in O(N + (N/B) log 4) time and emits at most four observations per bucket, O(N/B) output space. Python slices hold up to O(B) temporary items. It assumes strictly increasing timestamps and one continuous segment; production data with same-time events needs an explicit tie policy, and gaps need separate segments. Maintaining a pyramid of levels increases storage but can make viewport requests proportional to visible resolution rather than total history.

Common Mistakes

  • Taking every nth reading and deleting a short-lived alarm spike.
  • Reducing across a missing-data gap and drawing a continuous line.
  • Calling a retained minimum or maximum a bucket average.
  • Caching a reduced level without the filter and source-version keys.

Validation drill

Reduce a 47,000-point sensor series to a 900-pixel view. Insert 19 one-point spikes at varied bucket positions and verify every spike survives the chosen display reduction; compare load and pan times with the raw series.
